key_factors: (b) essential character of the solar cells
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the crystalline silicon photovoltaic solar cells in China
flip: Manufacturing the photovoltaic solar cells in Mexico
reasoning: The solar panels are classified in heading 8541 (8541.43). Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the tariff shift rule for heading 8541 in 102.20 requires a change from any other subheading outside 8541. As established in precedent H266527, assembling imported solar cells (also classified in heading 8541) into solar panels in Mexico fails the required tariff shift. Under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b), the foreign solar cells do not undergo the shift and impart the essential character, conferring Chinese origin.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the US cereal flakes
decisive_step: Production of the cereal flakes in the United States
flip: Sourcing the cereal flakes from Canada instead of the United States
reasoning: The cereal is classified in heading 1904 (prepared foods obtained by swelling/roasting cereals or unroasted cereal flakes/mixtures). Under 19 CFR 102.20, the rule for 1904 requires a change to heading 1904 from any other heading. All foreign ingredients made in outside headings shift to 1904 in Canada except the US-origin cereal flakes (already classified in 1904). Because the cereal flakes are the only foreign material that fails the tariff shift, under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b)(1)(i), they impart the essential character, making the origin the United States.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 2208.50
decisive_step: Macerating neutral grain alcohol with juniper and botanicals and re-distilling in Canada to produce gin
flip: If the botanical maceration and distillation into gin occurred in the Netherlands and Canada only diluted the gin with water and bottled it.
reasoning: The finished gin is classified in subheading 2208.50. The foreign 192-proof neutral grain alcohol from the Netherlands is classified in heading 2207 (undenatured ethyl alcohol of 80% vol or higher). Under 19 CFR 102.20(d) for 2208.10-2208.90, the required shift is a change to subheading 2208.50 from any other subheading except from 2207.10-2207.20 by simple dilution with water or other substances. Because the alcohol is macerated with juniper/botanicals and re-distilled in Canada (not mere dilution), it shifts under 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8421.29
decisive_step: Drilling the casing, installing the mesh jacket and centralizer, and welding them into the finished filter in Canada
flip: If the mesh jacket imported from Country A were already classified under subheading 8421.29 as an incomplete filter under GRI 2(a), it would fail the shift and Country A would confer origin under 102.11(b).
reasoning: The finished proMESH is classified in subheading 8421.29.00. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the applicable 102.20(o) rule for 8421.11-8421.39 requires a change from any other subheading. The foreign materials imported into Canada are the mesh jacket (8421.99.01), centralizer (Chapter 73), and L-80 casings (Chapter 73/78). In Canada, the casings are perforated and assembled/welded with the mesh jacket and centralizer into the finished filter. All foreign materials shift from other subheadings to 8421.29, so Canada is the country of origin.

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the aluminum alloy sheet/coil
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the 3105 aluminum alloy sheets in coils in China
flip: Further fabricating or assembling the aluminum sheets in Canada into identifiable swimming pool parts classifiable in subheading 9506.99 would satisfy the tariff shift and confer Canadian origin under 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: CBP rejected classification under 9506.99.5500 because the imported panels are merely rectangular aluminum alloy sheets (0.60 mm thick) with notched corners, classified in heading 7606 (7606.12). In Canada, Chinese 7606.12 coils are slit, painted, cut-to-size, and corner-notched. Under 19 CFR 102.20(n), heading 7606 requires a shift from any other heading; since both the coil and finished sheet fall in heading 7606, 102.11(a)(3) fails. Under 102.11(b)(1), the single material imparting essential character is the Chinese aluminum coil (cf. N316780, N316637).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift of foreign materials into the disassembled wine rack kit in Canada
decisive_step: Manufacturing the panels, applying the vinyl skin to the acrylic panel, and packaging the disassembled wine rack kit in Canada
flip: Sourcing the pre-cut panels and aluminum pegs as finished wine rack parts from China and merely packaging them in Canada
reasoning: The VINdustry Peg and Panel kit assembles into a wall-mounted wine bottle rack. Under GRI 2(a) and GRI 3(b), the unassembled composite good is classified as a completed rack (typically under heading 7615, 3924, or 4420 depending on the component imparting essential character, as determined in N336902). The processing in Canada, including fabricating the MDF/acrylic panels and affixing the decorative vinyl skin, satisfies the 19 CFR 102.20 tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) (or 102.11(b)(1) via the Canadian panels).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 2106.90 (or Chapter 17 syrup)
decisive_step: Processing, blending, and bottling of the cane sugar, maple syrup, and other ingredients into pancake and waffle syrup in Canada
flip: If the final syrup preparation classified in 2106.90 contained 65% or more by dry weight of foreign Chapter 17 sugar and the cane sugar failed the tariff shift, origin would be determined by the country of origin of the cane sugar under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: The Maple Treat Corporation processes the 'Maple Blend 3' pancake and waffle syrup in Canada using domestic and foreign ingredients (62.70% cane sugar, 29.63% water, 7% maple syrup, salt, and natural flavoring). Whether classified in subheading 2106.90 (where sugar is 62.70%, which is less than the 65% ceiling under 19 CFR 102.20(d)) or in heading 1702 via refining/blending in Canada (as in N328973 and N326397), the foreign ingredients undergo the required tariff shift in Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character of the Chinese heat-dissipating components (or non-qualifying simple assembly under 102.20 / 102.17)
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the specialized heat sink components (fins, heat pipe, vapor chamber, base, and plate) in China
flip: Manufacturing the heat pipes, vapor chamber, and stamped fins from raw metal stock in Mexico rather than importing pre-formed components from China
reasoning: Although the components are classified outside heading 8473 or under 8473.30, the Mexican processing consists merely of soldering pre-formed, dedicated Chinese components (fins, heat pipe, vapor chamber, base, plate) together in an oven. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and 102.17, simple assembly of pre-manufactured parts already dedicated to the finished heat sink (or classified in heading 8473) fails to meet the tariff shift. Under 102.11(b), the Chinese components impart the essential character, making the origin China.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum Cover Casting and Main Board Casting
decisive_step: Casting and forming of the aluminum cover and main board castings in South Korea
flip: Cast and form the aluminum cover and main board castings in Mexico
reasoning: The adapter plate assembly is a passive fluid conduit and mounting plate for a battery-electric passenger vehicle, classified in heading 8708 (8708.99) or 7616.99. In Mexico, South Korean custom-cast aluminum Cover and Main Board Castings are merely bolted together with a Mexican gasket, screws, and Chinese dowel pins. Because the Korean castings are already dedicated parts of the same heading (or assembled by simple fastening under 19 CFR 102.17), they fail the 102.20 tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b), the South Korean castings impart the essential character.

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character imparted by the non-shifting steering subheading 8708.94 components (rack bar and pinion)
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the core steering components (such as the rack bar and pinion gear) in South Korea
flip: Manufacturing or machining the rack bar and pinion gear in Mexico from raw steel bars of another heading so that all foreign components undergo the required tariff shift in Mexico
reasoning: The Manual Rack and Pinion Gear (MRP) is classified in subheading 8708.94, HTSUS. Under 19 CFR 102.20(p), the rule for 8708.94 requires a change from any other subheading. Because foreign steering components (such as the rack bar and pinion gear from South Korea) are already classified in 8708.94, they fail the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3) when assembled in Mexico (similar to N301716). Under 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b), the rack and pinion components impart the essential character, conferring South Korean origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7610
decisive_step: Extrusion, cutting, welding, and manufacturing of aluminum billets into structural components and cutting/sewing of fabric in Canada
flip: If the aluminum structural frame components were extruded and fabricated in Turkey and merely packaged with the fabric in Canada, origin would be Turkey.
reasoning: CBP rejects heading 6306 because the canopy is a permanent freestanding aluminum structure without walls, classifying it under heading 7610 (aluminum structures). Under 19 CFR 102.20, heading 7610 requires a change from any other heading. Turkish aluminum billets (7601), U.S. fabric, and other foreign components all undergo the required tariff shift in Canada via extrusion (consistent with N325521 and N326606), cutting, welding, and sewing. Thus, Canada is the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 3824
decisive_step: Mixing and blending of chemical and mineral ingredients in Canada
flip: If one of the foreign ingredients were already classified as a chemical preparation of heading 3824, the tariff shift in Canada would fail.
reasoning: Lubrigel L is a prepared drilling fluid additive containing 50.75% mineral oil (not predominant at >=70% for heading 2710), xanthan gum, guar powder, organoclay, and surfactant, classified as a chemical preparation in heading 3824. The product is neither wholly obtained nor made exclusively from domestic materials in Canada. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and 102.20, all foreign inputs (classified in headings 2710, 3402, 6806, 3913, and 1302) undergo the required tariff shift to heading 3824 when blended in Canada.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the LDPE drip lines
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the perforated LDPE drip lines in the United States
flip: Produce the LDPE drip lines in Mexico or Chile, or incorporate irrigation fittings/valves so the finished good classifies in heading 8424, allowing all Chapter 39 components to undergo a tariff shift in Mexico under 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: As a composite good of U.S. perforated LDPE drip lines (heading 3917) and Chilean LDPE film/sleeves (3920/3917) without mechanical fittings (excluding 8424), the IMT is classified under GRI 3(b) in heading 3917 (or 3926) based on the drip lines' essential irrigation function. Under 19 CFR 102.20, heading 3917 requires a shift from another heading (and 3926 from another chapter). The U.S. drip lines fail to shift in Mexico under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b)(1), the drip lines impart the essential character, conferring U.S. origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 1605
decisive_step: Wrapping the frozen scallop medallions in raw bacon in Canada
flip: If the scallop medallions were already prepared or preserved under heading 1605 when imported into Canada, they would fail the tariff shift and China would be the country of origin under 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: Following precedent N326450, frozen raw bacon-wrapped scallop medallions (45% scallop, 55% bacon) are classified under heading 1605 (subheading 1605.52) as prepared or preserved scallops because they are combined with bacon beyond Chapter 3 processes. The frozen scallop medallions imported from China are classified in heading 0307 (or if formed with binder as in N326450, undergo the shift or are Domestic/Canadian processed). Under 19 CFR 102.20(c), a change to heading 1605 from any other chapter is satisfied in Canada under 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character of the inner and outer races/rings
decisive_step: Machining and production of the toothed inner and outer rings in China
flip: Machining the raw forgings into toothed slewing rings in Mexico (or the assembly country) so that all foreign inputs undergo the required tariff shift to subheading 8483.40 under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: Toothed slew rings are classified as gears/gearing under subheading 8483.40, HTSUS (per HQ 083066). Under 19 CFR 102.20(o), subheading 8483.40 requires a tariff shift from any other subheading, or from 8483.90 under certain conditions. Because the imported Chinese toothed rings are already finished or unfinished gear elements or parts failing the required shift (or under 102.11(b) if assembled in Mexico from Chinese rings), the Chinese inner and outer toothed rings impart the essential character under 19 CFR 102.11(b).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 8443 and substantial transformation of components into finished printers
decisive_step: Manufacture of the PCBA, imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge in Mexico, and their integration with the Chinese printer transport and firmware in Mexico
flip: Manufacture the imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge in China and include them in the imported printer transport as in H304677
reasoning: Unlike in H304677 where the Chinese printer transport contained almost all mechanical printing components, here the imaging unit, developing unit, and toner cartridge are removed from the Chinese transport and manufactured in Mexico along with the controller PCBA (via SMT/PTH) and firmware loading. In Mexico, foreign parts undergo a tariff shift to heading 8443 under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and a substantial transformation, as the Chinese transport lacks core electrophotographic printing subassemblies that are now produced and integrated in Mexico.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum wine pegs
decisive_step: Manufacture of the aluminum wine pegs in India
flip: Manufacturing the aluminum wine pegs in Canada
reasoning: Following precedent N337479 (and N336902), which involved the identical 3-foot VINdustry Peg and Panel kit with the same component and value ratios, the unassembled composite good is classified under heading 7615 (or 9403) where the aluminum pegs impart the essential character. Because gathering kit components and affixing a decorative vinyl skin in Canada does not satisfy the 19 CFR 102.20 tariff shift for all foreign materials under 102.11(a)(3) (per 102.17), origin is determined under 102.11(b) by the Indian-origin aluminum pegs.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 3206.11
decisive_step: Surface treatment, drying, and grinding of Chinese titanium dioxide into pigment in Canada
flip: If the titanium dioxide imported from China into Canada had already been surface-treated or formulated as a pigment of subheading 3206.11, it would fail the tariff shift and China would confer origin under 102.11(b)(1).
reasoning: The finished surface-treated Titanium Dioxide Pigment (>80% titanium dioxide) is classified in subheading 3206.11, HTSUS. The intermediate unmixed titanium dioxide produced in China is classified in heading 2823.00, HTSUS. For 3206.11, 19 CFR 102.20 requires a change from any other subheading. Because the Chinese titanium dioxide shifts from heading 2823 to subheading 3206.11 via surface treatment and processing in Canada (compare N334326 on 3206.19), the country of origin is Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7326
decisive_step: Slitting, stamping, perforating, and assembling the stainless steel strip and screw into hose clamps in Canada
flip: Import pre-formed bands and housings of heading 7326 from India into Canada for simple assembly with the Chinese screw.
reasoning: Stainless steel worm-drive hose clamps are classified under heading 7326 (specifically 7326.90). Under 19 CFR 102.20(n), the rule for heading 7326 requires a change from any other heading, except from heading 7325. The foreign materials are flat-rolled stainless steel coils from India (heading 7220) and screws from China (heading 7318). In Canada, both foreign inputs undergo the required tariff shift to heading 7326 through slitting, progressive die stamping, perforating, and assembly. Thus, origin is Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b) essential character of the polyethylene film
decisive_step: Manufacturing and printing the polyethylene film in China
flip: Manufacturing the plastic spouts in Mexico or another country outside heading 3923 so all foreign materials shift to 3923.21 in Mexico under 102.11(a)(3)
reasoning: The finished polyethylene pouch with spout is classified in subheading 3923.21. In Mexico, Chinese polyethylene film (heading 3920 or 3921) is cut, heat-sealed, and combined with a Chinese plastic spout (subheading 3923.50). The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 3923 requires a change from any other heading. While the film shifts from 3920/3921, the spout is already in heading 3923 and fails the shift. Under 102.11(b), regardless of whether the film or spout imparts the essential character, both originate in China.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the unfinished valve blank
decisive_step: Electric upsetting and extrusion of the bar stock into the rough shape of the valve blank in China
flip: Perform the electric upsetting and extrusion of raw bar stock into valve blanks in Mexico instead of China
reasoning: Engine intake and exhaust valves are classified in heading 8409 (8409.99). In China, raw steel bar is stamped via electric upsetting and extrusion into the approximate shape of the finished valve (a valve blank), which is classified as an unfinished valve under heading 8409 pursuant to GRI 2(a). The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 8409 requires a change from another heading. Because the Chinese blank does not shift headings in Mexico, 102.11(b)(1) confers Chinese origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7610
decisive_step: Extrusion, cutting, tapping, welding, and powder coating of Turkish aluminum billets into the aluminum canopy framework in Canada
flip: If the aluminum posts and beams were already extruded and fabricated into structural parts of heading 7610 in Turkey and merely packaged with fasteners in Canada
reasoning: The freestanding aluminum canopy framework (imported without its fabric cover) is classified as an aluminum structure under heading 7610. The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 7610 requires a change from any other heading. In Canada, the Turkish aluminum billets of heading 7601 are extruded, cut, tapped, welded, and powder coated into structural posts and beams of heading 7610. Consistent with N339969, all foreign materials satisfy the required tariff shift in Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8471.70
decisive_step: Assembly and interconnection of the nine magnetic tape storage modules and robotic mechanism into the Serverless Rack cabinet by BDT de México in Mexico
flip: If the constituent storage modules were already classified in subheading 8471.70 prior to assembly in Mexico, or if assembly occurred through simple assembly of foreign 8473 parts
reasoning: The Serverless Rack lacks a CPU/server (unlike NY N342790) and functions solely as a mass magnetic tape storage unit under Chapter 84 Note 6(C), classifying it in subheading 8471.70 (storage units) rather than 8471.50. Under 19 CFR 102.20(o) for 8471.60-8472.90, a change to 8471.70 from any other subheading (or from 8473 provided it is not simple assembly) confers origin. Complex assembly and integration of the modules and robotics at BDT de México satisfies 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), making Mexico the origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8708.22 (or 7007.21)
decisive_step: Heating, pressing/bending, annealing, and laminating the flat glass with connectors and sensors into a finished automotive windshield in Mexico
flip: Import already-bent and laminated windshield glass from China into Mexico solely for attaching minor brackets and sensors
reasoning: The finished automotive windshield is classified under subheading 8708.22 (or 7007.21 if unframed). The Chinese flat glass (heading 7005) and other foreign components (primers, adhesives, sensors, brackets) are imported into Mexico, where the flat glass is heated to 634°C, press-bent to dual-axis curvature, annealed, laminated, and assembled with hardware. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and 102.20, all foreign materials undergo the required change in tariff classification in Mexico, making Mexico the country of origin for marking purposes.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the single material (nickel powder)
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the pure nickel powder by hydrometallurgy in Australia
flip: Ship unwrought nickel or nickel mattes (headings 7501 or 7502) from Australia to Canada and convert them into nickel powder (7504.00) in Canada.
reasoning: The finished pure nickel powder is classified in subheading 7504.00.00, HTSUS. In Canada, Australian-origin nickel powder (also 7504.00.00) is merely screened, sized, blended, and packaged. Under 19 CFR 102.20(n), heading 7504 requires a shift from any other heading, or from flakes to powder. Because the material starts and ends as nickel powder of 7504.00, it fails the tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b)(1), the single material imparting the essential character is the Australian nickel powder, making the origin Australia.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the raw carbon steel forging
decisive_step: Heating, forging, and heat-treating the steel billets into rough forgings in the shape of flanges and fittings in China (or Italy or India)
flip: Importing raw steel billets (heading 7207) into Mexico and performing the forging operation there so the steel undergoes a tariff shift to heading 7307 under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: The finished carbon steel flanges, crosses, and tees are classified in heading 7307. The rule in 19 CFR 102.20 for 7307 requires a change to heading 7307 from any other heading. Because the rough forgings imported into Mexico already have the approximate shape of the finished goods, they are classified as unfinished fittings/flanges in heading 7307 under GRI 2(a) (or fail the Chapter 73 Note matching 7307.91). Since the forgings fail the shift under 102.11(a)(3), origin is determined by the single material imparting essential character under 102.11(b): the forging from China, Italy, or India.

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the flat-rolled nonalloy steel coils
decisive_step: Melting, pouring, and manufacturing the flat-rolled nonalloy steel coils in Brazil
flip: Further processing the sheets in Mexico so they are prepared for use in a structure of heading 7308 (allowing a tariff shift from heading 7210/7212 to 7308 in Mexico)
reasoning: The roll-formed angular profile steel sheets are classified under heading 7216 (specifically 7216.91, cold-formed from flat-rolled products). The 19 CFR 102.20 rule for heading 7216 requires a change from any other heading, except from headings 7208 through 7215. Because the Brazilian flat-rolled painted/galvanized coils are classified in heading 7210 or 7212, they fail the required tariff shift in Mexico under 102.11(a)(3). Under 102.11(b)(1), the single foreign material (the Brazilian steel coil) imparts the essential character, making Brazil the country of origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8507.90
decisive_step: Manufacturing the cylindrical battery can assembly in Mexico from Korean steel, rivet, and gasket
flip: If the Korean steel were already formed into an unfinished battery can or part classified in heading 8507 prior to export to Mexico, it would fail the tariff shift and origin would be South Korea under (b).
reasoning: The finished 4680 Cylindrical Can Assembly is classified under subheading 8507.90.8000. It is not wholly obtained (102.11(a)(1)) or made exclusively from domestic materials (102.11(a)(2)). Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the applicable 102.20 rule for subheading 8507.90 requires 'A change to subheading 8507.90 from any other heading.' The Korean-origin inputs—raw steel (Chapter 72), rivet (Chapter 73/83), and gasket (Chapter 39/40)—are all classified outside heading 8507 and undergo the required tariff shift during production in Mexico.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) polymers
decisive_step: Production of the TPV polymer inputs in Japan
flip: Source at least 40% by weight of the total polymer content from the processing country (e.g., Mexico) and ensure no foreign input remains in heading 3902.
reasoning: The finished propylene elastomer is classified in subheading 3902.30.00. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), the 102.20 rule for headings 3901-3915 requires a change from any other heading, provided that the domestic polymer content is no less than 40% by weight of the total polymer content. Because 100% of the polymer inputs (TPV, polypropylene, propylene/ethylene/styrene-butadiene copolymers) originate in Japan, the domestic polymer content in China, Taiwan, or Mexico is 0%, failing the shift. Under 102.11(b), the Japanese TPV imparts the essential character.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 8414.30
decisive_step: Manufacturing the stator and rotor and assembling the foreign compressor parts into a finished hermetic compressor in Mexico
flip: Import an unassembled compressor kit from China that already has the essential character of a complete compressor classified in 8414.30 under GRI 2(a)
reasoning: The finished hermetic compressors are classified in subheading 8414.30. Under 19 CFR 102.20(o), the required tariff shift for subheadings 8414.10-8414.80 is a change from any other subheading, including another subheading within that group. The foreign components from China, India, and the U.S. (raw materials, parts in 8414.90, or other headings) are manufactured into stators and rotors and assembled into finished compressors in Mexico. Each foreign material shifts to 8414.30, conferring Mexican origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) (cf. H318255).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 1905.90 or 2106.90
decisive_step: Preparation, assembly, and freezing of the breakfast sandwich wrap in Canada
flip: If the wrap were classified in heading 1905 (e.g., 1905.90) where the 102.20 rule requires a change from any other heading, the U.S.-origin baked wheat lavash (also heading 1905) would fail the tariff shift, shifting the analysis to 102.11(b).
reasoning: The frozen breakfast wrap (filled with egg whites, cheeses, and vegetables in lavash) is a food preparation of heading 2106.90 (or 1901.90/1602). Under 19 CFR 102.20, subheading 2106.90 requires a change from any other subheading. All foreign ingredients (lavash of 1905, spices of Ch. 7/9, vegetables of Ch. 7/20, whey/starch of Ch. 4/35, citric acid of Ch. 29) are classified outside 2106.90 and undergo the required tariff shift when assembled in Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 9401.39
decisive_step: Manufacturing and assembly of the chair components in Mexico
flip: Importing the seat parts classified under subheading 9401.99 already formed from China without further manufacture beyond simple assembly
reasoning: The WP1000 Mesh Chair is a swivel seat with variable height adjustment, other than of wood, classified in subheading 9401.39, HTSUS. Under 19 CFR 102.20(r), the rule for subheadings 9401.10-9401.80 requires a change to subheading 9401.10 through 9401.80 from any other subheading, including another subheading within that group. Foreign raw materials and parts (such as subheading 9401.99 parts, fabrics, foam, metal, and plastics) undergo the required tariff shift to 9401.39 during manufacturing in Mexico under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (a)(1) wholly obtained or produced in a single country
decisive_step: Collection of the horse semen from stallions in Canada
flip: If the semen were collected from stallions located in another country and merely packaged into syringes in Canada, the origin would be the country where the semen was collected.
reasoning: Under 19 CFR 102.1(g)(4), products obtained from live animals in a country are considered 'a good wholly obtained or produced' in that country. Because the horse semen is collected from stallions in Canada and imported from Canada without foreign materials added, it is wholly obtained or produced in Canada. Therefore, pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(a)(1), the country of origin of the horse semen is Canada.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the bulk Parmesan cheese
decisive_step: Production of the bulk Parmesan cheese wheels in Wisconsin, United States
flip: Produce the bulk Parmesan cheese in Canada instead of the United States.
reasoning: The shredded/shaved Parmesan cheese is classified in heading 0406. Under 19 CFR 102.20, heading 0406 requires a change from any other heading, except from Canadian-produced fluid milk of 0401 or 0403. The U.S.-origin bulk Parmesan cheese (already heading 0406) is merely shredded or shaved and packaged in Canada, so it fails to undergo the required tariff shift under 102.11(a)(3). Moving to 102.11(b)(1), the U.S.-origin bulk cheese is the single non-shifting material that imparts the essential character of the product.

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the single material failing the tariff shift (plywood substrate)
decisive_step: Manufacture of the 8mm-thick hevea plywood substrate in Indonesia
flip: Import separate wood veneers (heading 4408) into Canada and laminate them into plywood there, satisfying the tariff shift to heading 4412 under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: The finished wood flooring is classified in subheading 4412.31. Under 19 CFR 102.20(i), heading 4412 requires a change from any other heading, or to surface-covered plywood (which requires obscuring the grain per Chapter 44 Additional U.S. Note 1(c)). The Indonesian plywood substrate (4412.31) fails the shift in Canada, whereas the U.S./Canadian face ply (heading 4407/4408) shifts. Under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b)(1)(iii), the Indonesian plywood substrate is the single material failing the shift and imparts the essential character.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8714.92
decisive_step: Cutting, laminating, molding, curing, and drilling carbon fiber sheets into bicycle rims in Canada
flip: If pre-molded unfinished rim blanks classified in subheading 8714.92 were imported into Canada from a third country and merely drilled and finished there.
reasoning: The finished carbon fiber bicycle rims are classified in subheading 8714.92, HTSUS. Under 19 CFR 102.20(p), the rule for subheadings 8714.91-8714.99 requires a change from any other subheading. The U.S.-sourced carbon fiber sheets (heading 6815) and any other raw materials (such as epoxy resin of heading 3907) are outside subheading 8714.92. Because all foreign materials undergo the required tariff shift during the cutting, molding, curing, and drilling in Canada, the country of origin is Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the sodium bentonite clay
decisive_step: Mining of the natural sodium bentonite clay in the United States
flip: Chemically activating the bentonite clay or adding chemical deodorizers/bactericides in Canada so the finished cat litter is classified in heading 3802 or 3824, allowing a tariff shift from heading 2508 in Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).
reasoning: Cat litter consisting of natural sodium bentonite clay mixed only with limestone and a water/cellulose dedusting agent remains classified in subheading 2508.10 (or heading 6815). key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 3824.99.49

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8433.11

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 8707
decisive_step: Assembly of the cargo container from component assemblies and parts in Mexico

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to headings 4811 and 3919 (or (b) essential character of the Chinese jumbo rolls where slitting from >20 cm to >20 cm rolls fails the shift)
decisive_step: Manufacturing, coating, and laminating the self-adhesive paper and polypropylene labelstock jumbo rolls in China

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the U.S. potato flakes

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to 9401.79.00
decisive_step: Assembly and manufacture of the Chinese metal leg assembly and U.S. plastic seat shell into a finished chair in Mexico

key_factors: (b) essential character of the brake caliper core

key_factors: (b) essential character of the PET film

reasoning: Following N331595, metallized PET film with coatings is classified in heading 3920. Under 19 CFR 102.20, a change to heading 3920 requires a change from any other heading. key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 3921

key_factors: (b) essential character of the sugar

key_factors: (b) essential character of the aluminum diecast armature and PU base wheel

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the carbonless paper

key_factors: (a)(1) wholly obtained or produced for hazelnut and flaxseed oils; (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 1515 for walnut oil

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 3926

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift or (b)(1) essential character of the molded insert base
decisive_step: Molding and forming of the hockey skate insert in China
flip: Manufacturing the molded base and assembling the insert in Canada from non-Chinese components
reasoning: The provided facts omit the specific countries of manufacture, materials, and tariff classifications for the hockey skate inserts. key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 4416 (or 4421)
decisive_step: Manufacturing and assembly of the oak staves and steel hoops into finished charred oak barrels in Mexico
flip: If the barrel staves and heads were pre-shaped and imported into Mexico as unassembled coopers' products of heading 4416 and merely assembled there, the tariff shift to heading 4416 would fail and origin would revert to the country of the oak components under 102.11(b).
reasoning: Under 19 CFR 102.20, goods of headings 4401 through 4421 (including coopers' products of heading 4416 and other articles of wood of heading 4421) require a change from any other heading, including another heading within that group. key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to heading 7112

Under 19 CFR 102.20(m), heading 7112 requires a change from any other heading. Because the foreign materials shift from heading 7108 to heading 7112 in Mexico, the country of origin is Mexico under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) (alternatively wholly obtained scrap in Mexico under 102.11(a)(1) per 102.1(g)(9)).

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8414.59
decisive_step: Final assembly of the fan blower components into a centrifugal fan blower assembly in Mexico
flip: Import an unassembled collection of components already classified as an incomplete fan in 8414.59 into Mexico for mere simple assembly, or perform the final assembly in China or Japan.
reasoning: The finished fan blower assembly is classified in subheading 8414.59.6560. Although the foreign housings and impeller are classified in heading 8414 (specifically parts under subheading 8414.90) and failed the stricter GN 11 USMCA heading-level shift, they successfully shift from 8414.90 (and the motor from heading 8501) to 8414.59 during assembly in Mexico.

key_factors: (b) essential character of the DC motor
decisive_step: Production of the 12 VDC motor in China

Proceeding to 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) and 102.18(b), the single non-shifting material—the Chinese DC motor—imparts the essential character to the actuator, conferring Chinese origin.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 9018.90 (or 9018.19)
decisive_step: Manufacturing the thermocouple subassembly (tinning, inserting constantan wire, laser welding dome) and assembling the RF probe in Mexico
flip: Importing a completed RF probe assembly into Mexico for mere attachment of the protective plastic sheath or packaging
reasoning: The RF probe is an electrosurgical/electro-medical instrument or part thereof classified in heading 9018 (specifically subheading 9018.90 or 9018.19, rather than 9018.39). None of the imported raw materials—stainless steel hypo-tubes (Ch. 73), insulated constantan wire and cable (8544), connectors (8536), solder, or plastic sheath (Ch. 39)—are classified in heading 9018. key_factors: (d)(2) simple assembly of foreign parts from a single country

reasoning: The doll and its parts are classified in heading 9503. In Mexico, all Chinese-origin molded ABS plastic components (head, torso, limbs, accessories) are merely screwed and glued together. Under 19 CFR 102.17(e), gathering parts classified as the finished good under GRI 2(a), or failing the 102.20 shift for 9503 due to parts remaining within 9503, disqualifies 102.11(a)(3). With no single component imparting essential character under (b), origin is China under 102.11(d)(2) (simple assembly of Chinese parts).

key_factors: (b)(1) essential character of the base belt
decisive_step: Manufacturing of the vulcanized rubber conveyor base belting in Taiwan
flip: Produce the base belting in Canada from unvulcanized rubber (heading 4005 or 4006) or textile fabric so it undergoes the required change of heading to 4010 in Canada
reasoning: The finished endless conveyor belts with sidewalls and drive lugs remain classified in heading 4010. Because the Taiwanese base belt is imported into Canada already classified in subheading 4010.12, it fails to undergo a change in heading. Moving to 102.11(b)(1), the base belt is the material that imparts the essential character to the finished conveyor belt, making the origin Taiwan.

key_factors: (a)(3) tariff shift to subheading 8708.99
decisive_step: Permanent press-fit assembly of the Taiwanese oil seal and Indian bearing cone in Mexico
flip: If the oil seal and bearing cone were merely packaged together as an unassembled set rather than permanently joined, the assembly would fail to shift to heading 8708 and origin would follow the individual components (Taiwan and India).
reasoning: Because the attached rubber oil seal imparts significant non-friction-reducing functions, the combined assembly is excluded from heading 8482 and classified as a motor vehicle part under subheading 8708.99. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) for the USMCA marking scenario (Mexico), the rule for 8708.99 requires a change from any other heading (or subheading). Both the Taiwanese oil seal (heading 4016) and the Indian bearing cone (subheading 8482.20) undergo the required tariff shift when permanently press-fitted together in Mexico.
